name: Decisions That Stay With People
title: Decisions That Stay With People
answer: AI can inform a decision about a child or an employee, but a named person makes that decision and can explain it. The rule matters because once a tool starts producing scores and flags that look official, it is easy to lose track of who actually decided. Keeping a person in the decision also gives families and staff a clear route to ask for a human review.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: This idea sets a boundary around what AI is allowed to do in a school. A tool may gather information, score work or raise a flag, but the decision itself belongs to a person who is named and who can account for the choice. The problem it solves is drift: scores and flags arrive looking official, and over time the machine's output quietly becomes the decision rather than one input to it. The book applies the rule to seven decisions that every school makes, which shows how widely it reaches. It also fixes the order of the work, so that human judgment comes first and the tool comes second.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day practice the order of the work is the part that matters most. People form their own judgment first, then use AI to check it, rather than letting the machine make the first call and asking a person to correct it afterwards. The Texas scoring program shows one version of this shared arrangement: an automated engine scores written answers first, people rescore about a quarter of them, and answers the engine is unsure about, or that are unusual, go straight to human scorers. The text does not divide this practice by grade band, so the same sequence applies wherever a tool touches a decision about a student or a member of staff. Buying a tool is treated as a decision about people as well, not only a purchasing choice.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no formal evidence label for the rule itself, so the support it gives is a set of studies and reported cases rather than a graded research base. In three online experiments with adults, when a machine made the first call and a person was supposed to correct it, people rarely fixed unfair decisions and often went along with them, while the problem went away when the person decided first and the machine served as the check (Krugel et al., 2023). The text notes that this study did not involve schools, but says the lesson travels. It also cites the Texas scoring program, where people rescore about a quarter of answers and unusual or uncertain ones go to human scorers (Texas Tribune, 2024), and the 2024 Los Angeles Unified chatbot, launched on a contract worth about $6 million, with about $3 million paid, and shut down within months when the vendor collapsed (EdSurge, 2024).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The main risk the text names is that people defer to a machine that goes first. When a tool makes the initial call, adults in the experiments rarely corrected unfair outcomes and often accepted them, which is why the sequence of judgment matters. Where AI touches a decision that matters, people need a clear way to ask for a human review, and the Texas case shows that even a shared scoring arrangement can leave educators questioning the results. The Los Angeles Unified story adds a second limit: a tool can disappear quickly, and families were left asking where student data had gone. The decisions themselves stay with people, and so does the responsibility for explaining them.
